topic: The reopened ticket problem in AI agent ROI

tweets.text: Your AI agent's resolution rate might be lying to you. Not on purpose. It just can't see what happens after the ticket closes.
tweets.headline: Your resolution rate might be lying

tweets.text: Agent answers a billing question. Customer says thanks. Ticket closes. That counts as a win in your dashboard right now.
tweets.headline: A closed ticket is not a win yet

tweets.text: Next morning the same customer writes in again. Same account, same charge, still wrong. A human has to clean it up this time.
tweets.headline: The customer comes back with the same problem

tweets.text: Two tickets exist in the system now. The first one is still sitting in the resolved column, exactly as it was the moment it closed.
tweets.headline: Two tickets now exist for one problem

tweets.text: Nothing in most reporting pipelines goes back and fixes that first count. The agent keeps the credit for a problem it never actually solved.
tweets.headline: The agent keeps credit it never earned

tweets.text: Resolution rate measures a moment, not an outcome. It tells you a chat ended without an escalation flag. It does not tell you if the fix held.
tweets.headline: Resolution rate measures a moment not an outcome

tweets.text: Closed and held are not the same claim. One is about timing. The other is about truth. Most ROI dashboards only ever check the first.
tweets.headline: Closed and held are different claims

tweets.text: This barely shows up for a simple agent. "What are your hours" rarely gets a comeback ticket because there is nothing left to get wrong.
tweets.headline: Simple agents rarely get comeback tickets

tweets.text: It shows up a lot once the agent handles refunds, account changes, multi step troubleshooting. Those closed tickets look identical. Until they are not.
tweets.headline: Complex agents close tickets that quietly reopen

tweets.text: Here is why nobody catches it. Most ticketing systems give a second contact a brand new ID unless someone manually links it back.
tweets.headline: Recontacts get a brand new ticket ID

tweets.text: And nobody is incentivized to go looking for that link. 👀 The agent team sees a healthy resolution count. Support sees an ordinary new ticket.
tweets.headline: Nobody is incentivized to find the link

tweets.text: Same unresolved problem, counted twice. Once as a win on the agent's scoreboard. Once as unrelated volume on somebody else's.
tweets.headline: One problem counted as two different wins

tweets.text: Now the cost math breaks too. The first pass gets logged at the agent's cheap cost per ticket.
tweets.headline: The first pass logs an artificially cheap cost

tweets.text: The second pass, the one a person actually has to fix, gets logged under regular support cost with zero reference back to the agent.
tweets.headline: The real fix cost gets buried elsewhere

tweets.text: So the ROI number does two bad things at once. It overstates what the agent fixed. And it understates what fixing it for real actually cost. 📊
tweets.headline: Your ROI number is wrong twice over

tweets.text: The fix is a held rate, not a closed rate. Link any repeat contact on the same issue within a window, say 72 hours, back to the original.
tweets.headline: Track a held rate not a closed rate

tweets.text: Only count the original as resolved if nothing bounced back in that window. Simple rule. Almost nobody applies it today.
tweets.headline: Only count it resolved if nothing bounces back

tweets.text: This is also a quality signal, not just a finance one. A held rate that stays steady as volume grows means a genuinely dependable agent.
tweets.headline: A held rate reveals real agent quality

tweets.text: A closed rate that stays flat while the held rate quietly drifts down is an early warning, long before it shows up in a satisfaction score. 🎯
tweets.headline: Quality decay shows up here first

tweets.text: We built agentworth's audit log to catch exactly this: every recontact linked back to the original, so a resolution only counts once it holds. Worth checking if yours does.
tweets.headline: Check if your ROI number actually holds
